Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

We started a mentorship program on the team this quarter. Six pairs, four months, one rule: mentees pick the topic each session.

The pairing process took longer than expected. We matched on stated interests first, then swapped two pairs after the kickoff call revealed a scheduling conflict. Lesson for next round: check calendars before matching on skills.

The first few sessions ran long on status updates. We fixed that by giving each pair a one-page prompt sheet — questions like "what's a decision you made this week you're unsure about" instead of "how's it going." Sessions got shorter and more useful at the same time.

One mentee, three weeks in, asked her mentor to review a design doc before it went to the team. That doc shipped with two fewer review rounds than her last one. That's the kind of outcome we were after: not a checklist of topics covered, but a habit of asking before you're stuck.

Not every pair found their rhythm. One pair meets biweekly and mostly talks about career goals. Another meets weekly and spends half the time on code review. Both count as working — the program didn't set an agenda beyond the first sheet.

We're extending it a second quarter and adding three more pairs. The prompt sheet stays. The forced weekly cadence goes — two of the six pairs asked to switch to biweekly, and we should have let them from the start.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (Six pairs, four months, one rule:):
- colon_reveal (Lesson for next round:):
- paragraph_uniformity (6 paragraphs, spread 0.27):

Return only the rewritten text.

One mentee, three weeks in, asked her mentor to review a design doc before it went to the team. That doc shipped with two fewer review rounds than her last one. Not a checklist of topics covered, but a habit of asking before you're stuck.

Not every pair found their rhythm. One pair meets biweekly and mostly talks about career goals. Another meets weekly and spends half the time on code review. Both count as working, since the program never set an agenda beyond the first sheet.

We're extending the program a second quarter and adding three more pairs. The prompt sheet stays. The forced weekly cadence goes: two of the six pairs asked to switch to biweekly, and we should have let them from the start.
